title: 2 Samuel 2:18–23
context: The three sons of Zeruiah are there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel, as light of foot as a wild gazelle, pursues Abner and does not turn to the right or to the left. Abner looks behind him, asks if it is Asahel, and is told that it is. He urges Asahel to turn aside to the right or the left, to seize one of the young men and take his armor, but Asahel will not turn away. Abner speaks again: he should turn away; why should Abner strike him to the ground, and how then could Abner look Joab his brother in the face? Asahel still refuses. Abner therefore strikes him with the back end of the spear, so that the spear comes out behind him; Asahel falls and dies in the same place, and all who come there stand still. Both traditions read the unit as a pursuit that ends in a kinsman’s death, told in plain sequence. Asahel’s speed and refusal, Abner’s warnings, and the manner of the blow are to be described as the text gives them, without being turned into a type of later vengeance or of some other story. The killing will hang over Joab and Abner in the chapters that follow; this passage itself records the death and the stillness at the place.

verses.text: The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel was as light of foot as a wild gazelle.
verses.arminianNotes:
The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel was as light of foot as a wild gazelle. The brothers are named, and Asahel’s speed is the trait that will drive the next verses.

Arminian readers hear a concrete introduction. Joab has already been in the field; now Abishai and Asahel are with him, and Asahel is compared to a wild gazelle, light of foot, before he begins the chase.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the three names and the gazelle comparison as the narrator’s preparation for the pursuit. Asahel’s swiftness is a fact of the story, not a symbol that needs to be decoded.

Both traditions read the verse descriptively, as the naming of Zeruiah’s sons and of Asahel’s speed, on shared ground.

verses.text: Asahel pursued Abner. He didn’t turn to the right hand or to the left from following Abner.
verses.arminianNotes:
Asahel pursued Abner. He didn’t turn to the right hand or to the left from following Abner. The chase is single-minded; the faster man holds a straight line after the beaten captain.

Arminian readers hear a real, stubborn pursuit. Asahel will not be shaken off to either side; the refusal to turn, which Abner will soon ask for, is already his path.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same straight following. Abner is in flight from a lost battle, and Asahel’s speed is used to stay on him without deviation.

Both traditions take the verse as the start of the hunt, shared narrative ground, without typological pressure on the right hand and the left.

verses.text: Then Abner looked behind him and said, “Is that you, Asahel?” He answered, “It is.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Then Abner looked behind him and said, “Is that you, Asahel?” He answered, “It is.” The pursued man looks back, names him, and is answered without disguise.

Arminian readers hear a moment of recognition. Abner knows who is behind him, and Asahel does not hide his name. The warnings that follow will be given to a man who has already identified himself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the question and the brief “It is.” as a clear meeting of identities in mid-pursuit. Abner is not striking a stranger in the dark; he knows it is Joab’s brother.

Both traditions read the verse as recognition, descriptive and shared, before the pleas of verses 21–22.

verses.text: Abner said to him, “Turn away to your right hand or to your left, and grab one of the young men, and take his armor.” But Asahel would not turn away from following him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Abner said to him, “Turn away to your right hand or to your left, and grab one of the young men, and take his armor.” But Asahel would not turn away from following him.

Arminian readers hear a way out offered and refused. Abner would have him take another opponent and another prize; Asahel will not turn away from this one man. The refusal is his own, and it will cost him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same offer and the same refusal. Abner tries to divert him to a lesser target; Asahel’s will is to follow Abner only.

Both traditions take the verse as a first warning, unheeded, and they describe it rather than turning the armor or the sides into symbols.

verses.text: Abner said again to Asahel, “Turn away from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I look Joab your brother in the face?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Abner said again to Asahel, “Turn away from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I look Joab your brother in the face?” The second plea names the blow and names Joab.

Arminian readers hear Abner already counting the cost. He does not claim to want Asahel’s death; he asks why he should strike him, and how he could face Joab. The warning is plain, and still it is only a warning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the second speech as a real attempt to stop the chase. Abner foresees a quarrel with Joab if Asahel falls by his hand. The next verse will show that the plea does not prevail.

Both traditions read the verse as a second, sharper warning, shared ground, without a typological reading of the face of Joab.

verses.text: However, he refused to turn away. Therefore Abner with the back end of the spear struck him in the body, so that the spear came out behind him; and he fell down there and died in the same place. As many as came to the place where Asahel fell down and died stood still.
verses.arminianNotes:
However, he refused to turn away. Therefore Abner with the back end of the spear struck him in the body, so that the spear came out behind him; and he fell down there and died in the same place. As many as came to the place where Asahel fell down and died stood still.

Arminian readers hear a refusal, a backward blow, and a death that stops those who come after. The back end of the spear still goes through him; he dies in the same place, and the pursuit of others pauses at the body. The manner of the stroke is as the narrator gives it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the “Therefore”: the refusal leads to the blow. Abner strikes with the butt of the spear, the spear comes out behind, and Asahel dies there. Those who come to the place stand still.

Both traditions take the verse as the end of this chase, a death that will not be forgotten in later chapters, but is here simply told, without being made a type of something else.
